message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10⁴³**.  

This estimate, often called the *Shannon number* after Claude Shannon, comes from a rough calculation that takes into account the branching factor of the game (≈30 moves per position) and the average length of a game (~80 plies). It gives a lower bound on the size of the search space that any exhaustive algorithm would have to explore.

In practice, more refined analyses suggest the true count of reachable legal positions may be closer to **10⁴⁶–10⁴⁷**, but the commonly cited figure remains 10⁴³.
